name: AI Governance & Risk
description: Responsible AI controls across the lifecycle, covering traditional ML and generative AI: governance and risk assessment, data and privacy, development and validation, AI-specific risks, access, change, monitoring and third-party AI.
references: NIST AI RMF 1.0, ISO/IEC 42001:2023, EU AI Act, OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025), MITRE ATLAS, SR 11-7

categories.name: AI Governance & Risk Assessment
categories.objective: AI use is known, approved through clear decision rights, owned, and risk-assessed before deployment.

items.control: An approved AI policy and generative AI acceptable-use standard define permitted and prohibited uses for in-house, vendor and employee AI use.
items.risk: Staff use AI in ways the organisation has not sanctioned, creating legal, ethical and security exposure.
items.test: Inspect the policy for approval, scope and defined prohibited uses, and confirm it was communicated and acknowledged by staff.
evidence: Approved AI policy and generative AI acceptable-use standard
All-staff communication or intranet publication record
items.other: NIST AI RMF GOVERN 1.2; ISO/IEC 42001 A.2

items.control: A cross-functional AI governance committee (legal, privacy, security, risk, data science, business) approves high-risk use cases under a charter.
items.risk: AI decisions are made in silos without legal, privacy, security and risk input.
items.test: Inspect the charter and minutes from three meetings; confirm quorum and that high-risk use cases were approved or rejected with recorded rationale and conditions.
evidence: Committee charter with membership and decision rights
Minutes recording use-case approvals and conditions
Decision log linked to the AI inventory

items.control: Each AI system has a named accountable business owner and a technical model owner.
items.risk: No one is accountable when an AI system causes harm.
items.test: For a sample of inventory entries, confirm both owners are named and still employed in a relevant role.
evidence: AI inventory with business and model owner fields

items.control: A central AI inventory covers in-house models, vendor-embedded AI features and generative AI tools, and is reconciled quarterly against discovery sources.
items.risk: Unregistered AI, including vendor features and staff GenAI use, escapes governance.
items.test: Compare the inventory to procurement records, the SSO app list and cloud AI service usage to identify unregistered AI.
evidence: AI inventory export with purpose, data, owner, risk tier and status
Reconciliation against procurement, SSO and cloud billing (e.g. Azure OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, Vertex AI usage)
Tickets registering newly discovered AI use

items.control: Every AI use case is assigned a risk tier (prohibited, high, limited, minimal) using documented criteria before development or purchase.
items.risk: High-risk AI gets the same light-touch review as low-risk tools.
items.test: For a sample of use cases, re-perform the tiering using the documented criteria and compare to the recorded tier.
evidence: Risk tiering criteria and decision tree
Completed tiering questionnaire per use case
Tier recorded in the AI inventory
items.other: EU AI Act Art. 6 and Annex III; AI RMF MAP 1.5

items.control: High-risk AI systems have an approved impact assessment covering effects on individuals, groups and society before go-live, including a fundamental rights impact assessment where required.
items.risk: Harms to people affected by the system are not identified before deployment.
items.test: For high-risk systems deployed in the period, confirm an impact assessment approved before the go-live date and that its mitigations were implemented.
evidence: Completed AI impact assessment (and FRIA where required)
items.other: ISO/IEC 42001 A.5; EU AI Act Art. 27; AI RMF MAP 5.1

items.control: New use cases are screened at intake against prohibited AI practices (e.g. social scoring, manipulative techniques, untargeted facial image scraping).
items.risk: The organisation deploys an AI practice that is banned or unlawful.
items.test: Inspect the intake form and confirm the prohibited-practice screen was completed for every use case registered in the period.
evidence: AI intake form with prohibited-practice questions
Legal review memos for borderline cases

categories.name: Data Protection & Privacy
categories.objective: Data used to train, ground and operate AI is lawful, minimised, protected and retained only as long as needed.

items.control: Provenance and usage rights (licence, consent, terms of use) are documented for training and fine-tuning datasets, and legal approves third-party or scraped data.
items.risk: Models are trained on data the organisation has no right to use, creating IP and privacy claims.
items.test: For a sample of models, inspect dataset documentation for source, licence or consent basis and legal approval.
evidence: Datasheets for datasets with source and licence
Legal approval for third-party or web-sourced data
items.other: EU AI Act Art. 10; ISO/IEC 42001 A.7

items.control: AI systems processing personal data have a DPO-approved DPIA, a documented lawful basis and implemented data minimisation.
items.risk: Personal data is processed by AI without a lawful basis or beyond what is necessary.
items.test: For AI systems processing personal data, confirm a DPIA approved before deployment and evidence that minimisation measures were built.
evidence: Record of processing entry for the AI system

items.control: Protected-attribute data used for fairness testing is held separately with access limited to named testers.
items.risk: Special-category data collected for bias testing is exposed or misused.
items.test: Inspect permissions on datasets containing protected attributes and confirm only named fairness testers have access.

items.control: Retention periods for prompts, outputs, vector stores and training snapshots are defined and enforced technically.
items.risk: AI data is kept indefinitely, extending breach impact and breaching retention rules.
items.test: Inspect retention settings for prompt logs, vector stores and training snapshots and compare them to the retention schedule.
evidence: Retention schedule entries for AI data types
Retention configuration for prompt logs and vector stores

items.control: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) indexes respect source permissions so users only retrieve documents they could open directly.
items.risk: The assistant reveals restricted documents to users who are not authorised to see them.
items.test: Query the assistant as a low-privilege test user for content from restricted sources and confirm it is not returned.
evidence: Permission-trimming configuration for the retrieval index
items.other: OWASP LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses

categories.name: Model Development & Validation
categories.objective: Models are built to a documented standard, tested realistically and independently challenged before use.

items.control: A model development standard requires a model card and reproducibility record (code commit, data version, environment) for each model.
items.risk: Models are built inconsistently and cannot be reviewed, reproduced or explained to regulators.
items.test: For sampled models, confirm a model card covering purpose, data, metrics, limitations and owner, plus a reproducibility record.
evidence: Reproducibility record linking commit, data version and environment
items.other: ISO/IEC 42001 A.6; EU AI Act Art. 11

items.control: Performance metrics and acceptance thresholds are approved before training, based on business risk tolerance.
items.risk: Models are judged good enough after the fact, against convenient metrics.
items.test: Confirm metric and threshold approval is dated before the training run, and that final results met the thresholds.
evidence: Metric and threshold approval dated before training
Rationale linking thresholds to business impact

items.control: High-risk models are independently validated (conceptual soundness, data, performance, limitations) before deployment.
items.risk: Errors and weak assumptions in high-risk models go unchallenged.
items.test: For high-risk models deployed in the period, inspect the validation report and confirm findings were resolved or accepted before go-live.

items.control: Models are tested on held-out data under deployment-like conditions, including edge cases, out-of-distribution inputs and perturbation.
items.risk: The model performs well in the lab but fails on real-world or unusual inputs.
items.test: Inspect the test plan and results for edge-case, out-of-distribution and stress scenarios, and confirm test data was held out from training.
evidence: Test plan covering edge cases and out-of-distribution scenarios
Results on the held-out evaluation set
items.other: AI RMF MEASURE 2.3, 2.5; EU AI Act Art. 15

items.control: The accountable business owner signs a go/no-go decision, including residual risk acceptance, before release.
items.risk: Models go live with residual risks nobody accepted.
items.test: For deployments in the period, confirm a signed go/no-go record dated before release and linked to the deployed model version.
evidence: Release record linking model version to approval

categories.name: AI-Specific Risks: Fairness & Transparency
categories.objective: AI outcomes are fair, explainable to the right degree, disclosed to the people they affect and open to challenge.

items.control: Bias testing across relevant groups uses defined fairness metrics and thresholds, and mitigation decisions are documented.
items.risk: The system produces discriminatory outcomes for protected groups.
items.test: Inspect the fairness report for the groups and metrics used, compare results to thresholds, and confirm mitigation decisions are documented.
evidence: Fairness test report (e.g. disparate impact ratio, equalised odds by group)
items.other: AI RMF MEASURE 2.11; NYC Local Law 144 (hiring tools)

items.control: Consequential decisions produce explanations (reason codes or feature attributions) suited to the audience.
items.risk: Decisions cannot be explained to customers, regulators or internal reviewers.
items.test: Request explanations for a sample of decisions and confirm they are produced, understandable and consistent with documented model logic.
evidence: Explainability method documentation (e.g. SHAP, reason code mapping)
Adverse action notice templates where applicable
items.other: AI RMF MEASURE 2.9; ECOA / Regulation B

items.control: People are told when they are interacting with AI, and AI-generated content is labelled.
items.risk: People do not realise they are dealing with AI or AI-generated content.
items.test: Walk through the user journey and confirm the AI disclosure appears before interaction and generated content carries a label or provenance metadata.
evidence: Screenshots of AI disclosure in the user interface
Content labelling or provenance configuration (e.g. C2PA metadata)

items.control: A system card or user guide states capabilities, accuracy, known limitations and the human oversight required.
items.risk: Users misuse the system because its limits are not communicated.
items.test: Inspect the system card for required content and confirm the published version matches the deployed model version.
evidence: Version history aligned to model versions
items.other: EU AI Act Art. 13; ISO/IEC 42001 A.8

items.control: People affected by automated decisions can contest them and obtain human review within a defined timeframe.
items.risk: People harmed by automated decisions have no way to challenge them.
items.test: Inspect the appeal procedure and, for sampled appeals, confirm a human review was completed within the timeframe.
evidence: Appeal log with outcomes and turnaround times
Customer-facing notice of the right to contest

categories.name: AI-Specific Risks: Reliability & Misuse
categories.objective: Generative and predictive AI outputs are reliable enough for their use, safe, lawful and not over-trusted.

items.control: Generative AI releases pass an evaluation suite for groundedness, factual accuracy and task success, including a human-reviewed sample.
items.risk: The system produces confident but false outputs (hallucinations) that users act on.
items.test: Inspect the evaluation suite and latest results against release thresholds, and the scored human-review sample.
evidence: Evaluation results for groundedness, citation accuracy and task success
Human review sample with scoring rubric
Release thresholds and pass or fail record
items.other: AI RMF MEASURE 2.5; OWASP LLM09 Misinformation

items.control: Content safety filters block toxic, unsafe and policy-violating inputs and outputs, and blocks are logged.
items.risk: The system generates harmful or brand-damaging content.
items.test: Inspect filter configuration, run a test set of harmful prompts and confirm they are blocked and logged.
evidence: Content safety configuration (e.g. Azure AI Content Safety, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails)

items.control: Use of AI-generated code and content is governed by policy, and code assistants block suggestions that match public code.
items.risk: AI-generated code or content infringes copyright or open-source licences.
items.test: Inspect the policy and the code assistant admin settings, and confirm vendor IP indemnity terms were reviewed by legal.
evidence: Policy on AI-generated content and code
Code assistant settings blocking public-code matches
Legal review of vendor IP indemnity

items.control: High-impact AI recommendations require documented human review, and override rates are monitored for rubber-stamping.
items.risk: Staff accept AI recommendations without meaningful review (automation bias).
items.test: Inspect the review procedure and monthly override-rate reports, and for sampled decisions confirm the reviewer recorded independent judgement.
items.other: EU AI Act Art. 14(4)(b); AI RMF MAP 3.4

items.control: Rate limits, token quotas and budget alerts are set on AI endpoints and agents.
items.risk: Abuse or runaway agents cause denial of service or uncontrolled cost.
items.test: Inspect rate limit, quota and budget alert configuration, and confirm alerts in the period were handled.
evidence: Cloud budget alerts for AI services

categories.name: AI-Specific Risks: Security
categories.objective: AI systems resist prompt injection, data leakage, poisoning and supply chain attacks.

items.control: High-risk AI systems are threat-modelled for prompt injection, data poisoning, model extraction and evasion.
items.risk: AI-specific attacks are not considered in design.
items.test: Inspect threat models for high-risk AI systems and confirm each listed attack class has a mitigation or accepted risk.
evidence: AI threat model mapped to MITRE ATLAS techniques

items.control: Input and output guardrails defend against direct and indirect prompt injection, and model output is validated before use in code, SQL, HTML or tool calls.
items.risk: Malicious input hijacks the model, or its output triggers unsafe actions downstream.
items.test: Inspect guardrail configuration and penetration test results for prompt injection, and review code that consumes model output for validation and encoding.
evidence: AI penetration test report covering direct and indirect prompt injection
Code review showing output validation and encoding

items.control: DLP and web controls stop confidential data and PII being sent to unapproved AI tools, and system prompts contain no secrets.
items.risk: Confidential data leaks through prompts to external AI services or through system prompt disclosure.
items.test: Inspect DLP and CASB rules for generative AI domains, review block events for the period, and inspect system prompts for embedded credentials.
evidence: DLP and CASB rules for generative AI domains

items.control: Models and ML libraries come from approved sources, third-party weights are scanned before use, and registry artefacts are hashed or signed.
items.risk: Tampered or malicious models or libraries are deployed (model supply chain attack).
items.test: Inspect the model registry for hashes or signatures and confirm third-party models in use were scanned and came from approved sources.
evidence: Model registry entries with artefact hashes or signatures
Model scanning results (e.g. unsafe serialisation checks)
Approved model and package source list
items.other: OWASP LLM03 Supply Chain, LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning

items.control: AI red-teaming is performed before release of high-risk systems and at least annually afterwards.
items.risk: Attackers find exploitable weaknesses before the organisation does.
items.test: Inspect red-team scope and report, and confirm high findings were fixed and retested before release or have accepted risks.
items.other: AI RMF MEASURE 2.7; EU AI Act Art. 15

categories.name: Access Control
categories.objective: Access to AI platforms, models, credentials and agent capabilities is limited to what is needed.

items.control: Access to ML platforms, training data and the model registry is role-based and reviewed quarterly.
items.risk: Unauthorised people alter models or extract training data.
items.test: Inspect role assignments on the ML platform, data stores and registry, and confirm quarterly review sign-off with removals actioned.
evidence: Role assignments on the ML platform (e.g. SageMaker, Vertex AI, Databricks)

items.control: AI provider API keys are stored in a vault, scoped per application and rotated.
items.risk: Leaked keys let others run up costs or access data under the organisation's account.
items.test: Inspect where provider keys are stored, confirm per-application scoping and rotation dates, and review secrets-scanning alerts.
evidence: Vault entries for AI provider keys with rotation dates

items.control: AI agents run with least-privilege identities, and write, payment or delete actions require human approval.
items.risk: An AI agent takes harmful actions using broad permissions (excessive agency).
items.test: Inspect the tool permission matrix and service identity permissions for each agent, and confirm high-impact actions route to human approval.
evidence: Human approval workflow configuration and logs

items.control: Approved generative AI tools are accessed through SSO on enterprise terms, and consumer AI accounts are blocked or warned on.
items.risk: Staff use personal AI accounts whose terms allow training on company data.
items.test: Confirm approved AI tools are behind SSO with enterprise data terms, and that web filtering blocks or warns on unapproved AI sites.
evidence: SSO configuration for approved AI tools
Web filter policy for the generative AI category

categories.name: Change Management
categories.objective: Changes to models, prompts and AI configuration are versioned, tested, approved and re-assessed.

items.control: New or retrained model versions are released through change control with evaluation results and approval.
items.risk: Retrained or modified models are released without testing or approval.
items.test: For model versions released in the period, confirm a change record with evaluation results and approval dated before deployment.

items.control: System prompts, retrieval settings and guardrail configuration are version-controlled, peer-reviewed and regression-tested before release.
items.risk: Prompt or configuration edits silently change system behaviour.
items.test: Confirm prompts and AI configuration live in version control, and that sampled changes have a reviewer and a regression evaluation run.
evidence: Pull request reviews for prompt changes

items.control: Material changes (new data source, new user population, new purpose, retraining) trigger re-assessment of risk tier and impact.
items.risk: Risk assessments go stale as the system's data, users or purpose change.
items.test: For systems with material changes in the period, confirm the tier and impact assessment were re-performed.

items.control: Retired models have endpoints disabled, data deleted or archived per retention, and inventory status updated.
items.risk: Retired models keep running, or their data is kept longer than allowed.
items.test: For models retired in the period, confirm endpoint shutdown, data disposition and inventory update.

categories.name: Monitoring & Logging
categories.objective: Deployed AI is monitored, traceable, overseen by people and supported by an incident process.

items.control: Production models are monitored for data drift, concept drift and performance degradation, with alert thresholds.
items.risk: Model performance degrades silently in production.
items.test: Inspect monitoring dashboards and thresholds, and for sampled alerts confirm investigation and action.
evidence: Drift and performance dashboards (e.g. Evidently, Arize, SageMaker Model Monitor)
items.other: AI RMF MEASURE 2.4; EU AI Act Art. 72

items.control: Inputs, outputs, model version, user and timestamp are logged for each inference and retained per policy.
items.risk: AI decisions cannot be traced or investigated.
items.test: Inspect the log schema and sample records for required fields, and compare retention settings to policy.

items.control: Operators can override, pause or roll back the AI system, and the kill switch is tested at least annually.
items.risk: Operators cannot stop or override the system when it misbehaves.
items.test: Inspect the oversight procedure and the record of a kill-switch or rollback test within the last 12 months.
items.other: EU AI Act Art. 14; AI RMF MANAGE 2.4

items.control: An AI incident playbook defines AI incidents and severity, escalation, and when serious incidents are reported to regulators.
items.risk: AI failures are not escalated, learned from, or reported when required.
items.test: Inspect the playbook and incident log; for sampled incidents confirm triage, root cause and any required notification.
evidence: AI incident playbook with definitions and severity levels
items.other: EU AI Act Art. 73; AI RMF MANAGE 4.3

items.control: User feedback on AI outputs is captured in-product and triaged weekly.
items.risk: Problems users notice never reach the team that can fix them.
items.test: Inspect the feedback mechanism and triage log, and confirm flagged outputs were reviewed and actioned.
evidence: In-product feedback mechanism (e.g. thumbs down with reason)

categories.name: Third-Party AI & Regulatory Compliance
categories.objective: AI from vendors is assessed and contracted appropriately, and applicable AI regulation is tracked and met.

items.control: AI vendors complete due diligence on model provenance, training data practices, security and data retention before contract.
items.risk: Vendors train on the organisation's data or operate weak AI controls.
items.test: For AI vendors onboarded in the period, confirm the AI questionnaire and data-use review were completed before contract signature.
evidence: AI vendor questionnaire covering model provenance, training data and retention
Vendor SOC 2 report or ISO/IEC 42001 certificate

items.control: AI contracts prohibit training on customer data without consent and cover IP indemnity, incident notification and audit or transparency rights.
items.risk: Contracts leave the organisation unprotected on data use, IP and incidents.
items.test: Check sampled AI contracts against the AI clause checklist.

items.control: Vendor model versions are pinned, and updates or deprecations trigger a regression evaluation before adoption.
items.risk: A vendor model update changes behaviour without warning.
items.test: Confirm model versions are pinned in configuration and a regression evaluation ran before each version change in the period.

items.control: Regulatory horizon scanning tracks applicable AI laws and guidance, with an applicability assessment for each new requirement.
items.risk: New AI obligations apply without anyone noticing.
items.test: Inspect the regulatory register for quarterly updates and applicability assessments for new requirements.
evidence: AI regulatory register (e.g. EU AI Act, Colorado AI Act, sector guidance)

items.control: A fallback (alternative model or manual process) is documented and tested for critical processes that depend on third-party AI.
items.risk: A provider outage halts business processes that depend on AI.
items.test: Inspect the fallback runbook and evidence of a failover or manual-process test in the last 12 months.
